frames.spoken_text: Welcome to Khan Academy’s study of mitosis. Cellular reproduction is the core biological process that allows multicellular organisms to grow, heal, and sustain life. Before any mechanical division can take place, the cell spends the vast majority of its life in interphase, carefully duplicating its entire genomic DNA and synthesizing proteins to prepare for nuclear fission.

frames.spoken_text: In prophase, diffuse chromatin fibers undergo dramatic structural condensation, coiling into tight, microscopically visible X-shaped sister chromatids. Simultaneously, the protective nuclear envelope begins to dissolve, and duplicated centrosomes push away from each other toward opposite poles, extending the microtubule fibers that will form the mitotic spindle.

frames.spoken_text: During metaphase, dynamic microtubule fibers attach to protein complexes called kinetochores located on each chromosome centromere. Molecular motor proteins generate opposing tension, pulling back and forth until every single chromosome aligns along the cell equator. The spindle assembly checkpoint actively monitors this alignment before permitting progression.

frames.spoken_text: Once the checkpoint verifies that every kinetochore is anchored under bidirectional tension, anaphase begins instantly. Protein cohesin rings holding sister chromatids together are cleaved by separase enzymes. Spindle fibers depolymerize rapidly, dragging the separated V-shaped chromatids toward opposing poles of the dividing cell.

frames.spoken_text: In telophase, the mechanical work of chromosome separation concludes. As the isolated chromosomes reach the cell poles, they decondense back into uncoiled chromatin. The mitotic spindle completely disassembles, and fresh nuclear envelopes reconstruct around each genomic cluster, creating two distinct nuclei within one cytoplasm.

frames.spoken_text: Finally, cytokinesis physically cleaves the cell into two independent entities. An actin-myosin contractile ring pinches the plasma membrane inward along the cleavage furrow. The membrane fuses shut, yielding two genetically identical diploid daughter cells, ready to enter interphase and begin the cycle anew.
